specPoints.text: explain the potential dangers of electrostatic charges, e.g. when fuelling aircraft and tankers (physics only)
explain some uses of electrostatic charges, e.g. in photocopiers and inkjet printers (physics only)

primer.text: Static electricity is a working tool in some machines and a hidden hazard in others. Photocopiers and inkjet printers steer charged toner and ink with charge forces; sprayers charge droplets so they spread evenly. The same build-up turns dangerous near flammable fuel, which is why aircraft get earthed with a bonding line during refuelling.

lessons.title: Uses: photocopiers & insecticide sprayers
lessons.opening: Photocopiers run a five-step charge choreography: project the page, let the lit areas lose their charge, dust the rest with negative toner, transfer it to paper, then heat it fixed. Inkjet printers charge their droplets for steering instead. Sprayers charge their output so droplets repel into a fine, wide-reaching mist.
keyPoints: Photocopiers project the page onto a positively charged plate.
Bright areas lose their charge; the dark text areas keep it.
Negatively charged toner powder sticks to the charged text and is heated onto blank paper.
Inkjet printers charge coloured ink droplets negatively so they land on the right spot.
Sprayed insecticide droplets are given like charges, so they repel into a fine mist.
Those repelled droplets also fall fast, attracted by Earth's opposite charge.

low.restatement: Charged ink and toner go where opposite charges wait; like-charged droplets push apart to spread a spray.
low.analogy: A magnet-controlled ping-pong ball: steer it by placing the attracting pole where you want it to land.
low.examPointer: Learn the photocopier steps in order — projection, discharge, toner, transfer, heat-fixing.

medium.restatement: Every use reduces to force control: attract where you want deposition, repel where you want dispersion.
medium.analogy: Traffic control with one rule: red signs attract cars to park, identical badge plates repel drivers into separate lanes.
medium.examPointer: Sprayer answers have two halves — repulsion spreads the mist, Earth's attraction speeds the fall.

check.stem: A photocopier's copying plate is charged:

options.explanation: The plate starts positive; the toner is the negative partner.

options.text: positively before the image is projected
options.explanation: Projection then discharges the lit regions, leaving the text areas positive.
The whole method rests on the plate's charge.
Nothing special happens at the edges.
Positive toner would be repelled by the positive text areas.
Uncharged powder would land everywhere.
The charge is fixed negative.

options.text: negative charge, so it sticks to the dark areas
options.explanation: Negative toner adheres exactly where the positive charge survived.

check.stem: Freshly copied paper feels warm because:

options.text: it was heated so the toner would stick
options.explanation: Heat-fixing is the final step of the copy process.
The lamp never touches the paper.
Repulsion would not warm anything.
Spinning does not heat the paper.

check.stem: Inkjet droplets are charged so they:

options.explanation: Charging has nothing to do with evaporation.
They are guided TO the paper.

options.text: are guided to the correct spot on the page
options.explanation: The charge lets the printer steer each droplet's landing place.
They are fired at the page.

check.stem: Charged insecticide droplets spread out because they:

options.explanation: Attraction would clump the spray.

options.text: repel each other, having the same charge
options.explanation: Like charges push the droplets apart into a fine mist.
Neutral droplets would not disperse this way.
No freezing occurs.

check.stem: Name two devices that use electrostatic charge.
check.modelAnswer: Photocopiers and inkjet printers — insecticide sprayers also qualify.

check.stem: Why does an electrostatic sprayer cover a large area?
check.modelAnswer: The like-charged droplets repel one another into a fine mist that also falls quickly toward the charged Earth.

check.stem: Explain why the toner only sticks to the text regions of the plate.
check.modelAnswer: The illuminated regions lost their charge, so only the dark text areas still hold positive charge that can attract the negatively charged powder.

check.stem: A car body is sprayed with positively charged paint droplets. Predict two effects of the charge.
check.modelAnswer: The droplets repel one another into an even mist, and they are attracted over to the earthed car body, coating it evenly with little waste.

lessons.title: Dangers: sparking when fuelling vehicles
lessons.opening: A big enough gathered charge jumps the gap: that jump is a spark, and near flammable vapour it is an explosion waiting for a match. Fuel rushing through a pipe charges itself by friction, so aircraft are wired to the Earth with a copper bonding line while they refuel — the charge drains away harmlessly.
keyPoints: A large gathered charge can spark across a gap once its voltage is big enough.
Sparks near flammable fuel vapour can start a fire or an explosion.
Fuel rushing through pipes gains charge by friction against them.
A bonding line — a copper wire to Earth — carries that charge away safely.
Charge prefers the bonding line's path, so sparking during refuelling becomes very unlikely.

low.restatement: Static builds up on fuel; a spark could ignite it; a wire to Earth lets the charge escape instead.
low.analogy: Letting a kettle boil slowly through a pipe rather than letting pressure build until it bursts.
low.examPointer: Danger answers name the spark, the ignition and the earthing fix — three sentences, three marks.

medium.restatement: The physics is a race: charge flows down the bonding line far more easily than it can force a spark through air, so the safe path wins every time.
medium.analogy: A fire exit next to a wall: everyone takes the open door, nobody dives through the brick.
medium.examPointer: State what the bonding line is made of — copper wire — as well as what it does.

options.explanation: Steady flow in a conductor is not a spark.
Gentle warming is not a spark.

options.text: a large voltage drives current across an air gap
options.explanation: Enough charge and voltage force current through the air — the spark.
Slow earthing is precisely what prevents sparks.

check.stem: Fuel flowing through a pipe gains charge because of:

options.explanation: Weight plays no role.
Colour is irrelevant.
Magnetism is not the charging mechanism.

options.text: friction between the fuel and the pipe
options.explanation: The rubbing of the liquid insulator on the pipe transfers charge to the fuel.

check.stem: The bonding line is made of:

options.explanation: The bonding line is a copper wire to Earth.
Rubber would insulate — the opposite of the goal.
Glass is an insulator.
Plastic is an insulator.

check.stem: The bonding line reduces the spark risk by:

options.explanation: No cooling is involved.
The wire gives the charge an easy path to Earth.
Pump speed is unaffected.
Insulating would trap the charge.

check.stem: The danger from a spark near flammable fuel is:

options.explanation: Frost is unrelated.
Batteries are not part of the hazard.

options.text: fire or explosion from a spark
options.explanation: A spark near flammable fuel can ignite it.
Paint is not the risk.

check.modelAnswer: Electrocution, for example from lightning, and fire or explosion when a spark meets flammable gas or liquid.

check.stem: What is a bonding line and what does it do?
check.modelAnswer: A copper wire connecting the aircraft's tank to Earth; it carries the gathered charge away so sparks cannot form.

check.stem: Explain why the fuel can gather charge as it is pumped.
check.modelAnswer: Fuel is a liquid insulator, so the rubbing against the pipe transfers and holds charge on it instead of letting it flow away.

check.stem: During a plane refuel, describe how the bonding line keeps the operation spark-free.
check.modelAnswer: The copper bonding line connects tank and Earth, so friction-gained charge drains down it; with an easier path than a spark, dangerous discharge is avoided.

glossary.definition: Current forced across an air gap by a large gathered charge.
The copper wire earthing an aircraft during refuelling, carrying charge away safely.
The negatively charged powder a photocopier deposits on the charged text areas.
Injury or death from electric current passing through a body.
